Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) helps people find solutions to their legal disputes without going to trial. The Court
offers a variety of ADR resources and programs
Parties may talk with each other about resolving their case at any time. If the parties have
attorneys, they will negotiate for their clients.
Mediation may be appropriate for parties who want to work out a solution but need help from a
neutral third party. A mediator can help the parties reach a mutually acceptable resolution. Mediation may be
appropriate when the parties have communication problems
or strong emotions that interfere with
resolution. Mediation may not be appropriate when the parties want a public trial,
or have a history of physical
Less formal than a trial, parties present evidence and arguments to an arbitrator who decides the
outcome. In "binding" arbitration, the arbitrator's decision is final; there is no right to trial. In "nonbinding"
arbitration, any party can request a trial
A judge or qualified settlement officer assists the parties in evaluating the strengths
and weaknesses of the case and in negotiating a settlement. Mandatory settlement conferences may be ordered
by a judicial officer. In some cases, voluntary settlement conferences may be requested by the parties.
Utilizing ADR methods is often faster than going to trial and parties can save on court
costs, attorney's fees, and other charges.
ADR is conducted outside of a courtroom setting and does not involve a
For many types of ADR, parties may choose their ADR process and provider.
If the parties do not resolve their dispute, they may have to pay for ADR, litigation, and trial.
ADR does not provide a public trial or decision by a judge or jury.

ADR Programs for Unlimited Civil (cases valued over $35,000)
Litigants should closely review the requirements for each program and the types of cases served.
Litigants in unlimited civil cases may use the Civil Mediation Vendor
Resource List to arrange voluntary mediations without Court referral or involvement. The Resource List includes
organizations that have been selected through a formal process that have agreed to provide a limited number of
cost mediation sessions with attorney mediators or retired judges. Organizations may accept or
decline cases at their discretion. Mediations are scheduled directly with these organizations and are most often
conducted through videoconferencing. The organizations on the Resource List target active civil cases valued
$250,000, though cases outside this range may be considered.
